content.subject: Decide which model governs the commercial numbers
content.description: Owner decision, nothing else can proceed past it. A1's probability-blended evaluation (0.05% catastrophic escalation, $500,000 typical cost) vs D08 §5–§6's contained-tier basis. Options costed in assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md §6–§7; recommendation is A1. Everything quoted to a customer depends on this.

content.subject: Restate the 2.0x/4.1x return anchors in A2 §3.2 and D08 §3
content.description: The anchors are recoverable at p between 0.04% and 0.07% on an unstated pilot-plus-three-years cost frame, so this is a disclosure defect not a fabrication. Either state the frame explicitly or strike them. Cannot ship unreconciled.

content.subject: Restate D08 §5–§6 from the governing model and fix the roi.py 29x defect
content.description: D08 §5–§6 run 5x–14x above A1 at identical inputs and contradict D08's own §4 (~$993,000 vs $8.6M–$11.4M). backend/roi.py values a missed defect at 29x A1 (2% probability and $9.25M contained cost, against 0.05% and $500,000).

content.subject: Regenerate the A1 workbook and re-run both check scripts
content.description: Deliberately deferred because regenerating bakes the undecided model into a new file. Once findings 1 and 2 are settled: node/python the corrected builder, then python3 -I assets/a2-d08-arithmetic-pass.py (78 figures) and python3 -I assets/a2-d08-model-decision.py (65 checks).

content.subject: Verify the off-box replication gap against B01 §7 item 12 and D09 §4.4–4.5
content.description: Do not build from the handoff note. Read B01 §7 item 12 and D09 §4.4–4.5, confirm nothing currently ships a bundle on a schedule, and record exactly what is missing.

content.subject: Build scheduled off-box replication of the signed ledger export
content.description: The signed export exists; nothing ships it. Needs a scheduled job, retention per D09 §4.5, a written key-custody procedure, and tests. The one build on the list needing no commercial decision and no new dependency. Can start now, in parallel with the blocked model chain.

content.subject: Independent adversarial audit of the replication work
content.description: Second agent with no stake, told to falsify rather than confirm, writing its own arithmetic and verifying quotes against source files. A green self-check proves internal consistency only — it cannot catch a wrong premise I also encoded in the check. This has earned its cost three times in two sessions.

content.subject: Update docket and commit the replication build
content.description: Update the docket docs the change touches (B01 §7 item 12, D09 §4.4–4.5, D00 Part IV/VI, README) in the same pass, write assets/ internal analysis, commit named files only with --ignore-cr-at-eol, never git add -A.

content.subject: D07 §14.5 governing law and venue — counsel decision
content.description: Governing law, seat and forum. Open counsel decision, correctly labelled as open. Blocks first execution but not formation. Requires a signed addendum — cannot be drafted closed by me.

content.subject: Snapshot and commit the chat-4 transcript at close
content.description: Extract with project-logs/extract_transcript.py, role is the top-level type field not message["role"]. Take the snapshot after the last exchange, not when the work feels finished. Both the .md and raw .jsonl into project-logs/transcripts/. Only call it preserved once committed.

# A2 — Rate Card & Band Definitions

**Docket position:** A2. The authoritative price schedule for every commercial document in this docket.

**Classification:** Client-facing. May be shown to the Railroad.

> **Drafting status:** Commercial grade. **This document supersedes every fee figure in D02, D05, and D08.** Where a fee in any other document differs from this schedule, this schedule governs for price (D00 Part IV, rule 4).
>
> **Effective date:** ______________________  **Version:** 1.0
> **Rate lock:** fees in this schedule are held for the duration stated in §8.

---

## 1. What this document is, and why it exists

Every contract in this docket needs to cite **one** place for price. Without that, the pilot agreement quotes one number, the rollover agreement quotes a second, and the licence document quotes a third. The first time a customer's procurement analyst puts all three side by side, the discrepancy becomes a negotiating lever against you.

This schedule is that one place. It states:

1. **What we charge for** — the units of measure.
2. **How much** — the bands and rates.
3. **What is included** at each level.
4. **What is not included** and therefore separately priced.
5. **When invoices are issued** and when they are due.

**Two pricing axes, and they measure different things.** The licence axis prices **assets** — how many freight car axles we monitor. The platform axis prices **geography** — how many physical places we install equipment at. These are genuinely different costs and collapsing them into one number is the mistake that makes corridor deployments unprofitable. See §4.

---

## 2. Definitions used in this schedule

**Monitored Axle.** One freight car axle from which the platform receives, processes, and produces advisories. An axle is counted once, regardless of how many times it passes a detector. Locomotive axles are not counted unless expressly agreed in an Order.

**Site.** One physical location where the platform is installed and maintained — one wayside detector location, or one classification yard with edge compute. A site requires its own edge server, detector integration, network path, commissioning, and support coverage.

**First Site.** The single site included in the base licence. Every additional site attracts the platform fee in §4.

**Pilot.** The fixed-term, single-site, evaluation engagement under D02.

**Production Licence.** An annual licence under D08, following conversion from a pilot under D05, or purchased directly.

**Order.** A Statement of Work under D04, executed under the MSA (D03).

**Band.** A marginal price tier. Axles are priced band by band, cumulatively — **not** at a single flat rate for the whole count. §3.2 explains why, and it matters to the customer.

**Commissioning Date.** The date the Railroad signs the Configuration Attestation (Form F02) confirming the platform is operational at a site.

**Business Day.** Monday to Friday, excluding US federal holidays.

---

## 3. Axis one — Per-axle licence

### 3.1 The bands

| Band | Axles in this band | Rate per axle per year | Cumulative annual licence at top of band |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| **Band 1** | First 500 axles | **$600** | $300,000 |
| **Band 2** | Next 1,500 axles (501–2,000) | **$500** | $1,050,000 |
| **Band 3** | Above 2,000 axles | **$375** | $2,175,000 at 5,000 · $4,050,000 at 10,000 |

### 3.2 Why the bands are marginal, not flat tiers

A flat tier structure charges a single rate for the whole axle count. That produces a cliff: a customer with 501 axles pays the 500–2,000 rate on **all 501**, so doubling their fleet more than doubles their bill, and their return on the platform gets **worse** as they expand.

That is the opposite of what a fleet-scale economics product should do. Marginal bands mean the rate falls as volume rises, the customer's modelled return improves monotonically with fleet size — approximately **1.8x at 500 axles, rising to about 3.4x at 10,000** — and expansion is rewarded rather than punished.

**The basis of those figures is stated here rather than left to inference:** net three-year benefit computed from the A1 model at its own defaults — a **0.05%** probability that a missed defect escalates to a catastrophic event, a **$500,000 typical** contained derailment cost, and the sourced $1,000,000,000 catastrophic cost — measured against the four-year fee commitment at list price with no conversion credit. It is a four-year cost basis against three years of benefit, which understates the return rather than inflating it. Recompute from A1 if any of those three inputs changes.

The customer will understand this the moment it is explained, and it is worth explaining, because a procurement analyst who spots what looks like a cliff will assume it is a negotiating tactic. It is not; it is a band structure, and the arithmetic in §3.3 shows it.

### 3.3 Worked calculation — the arithmetic a procurement analyst will do

**Example A — 500 axles, one site**

| | Axles | Rate | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Band 1 | 500 | $600 | $300,000 |
| Band 2 | 0 | — | $0 |
| Band 3 | 0 | — | $0 |
| **Licence subtotal** | | | **$300,000** |
| Site fee (first site included) | | | $0 |
| **Annual total** | | | **$300,000** |

**Example B — 1,000 axles, three sites**

| | Axles | Rate | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Band 1 | 500 | $600 | $300,000 |
| Band 2 | 500 | $500 | $250,000 |
| Band 3 | 0 | — | $0 |
| **Licence subtotal** | | | **$550,000** |
| Site fee (2 additional × $45,000) | | | $90,000 |
| **Annual total** | | | **$640,000** |

**Example C — 5,000 axles, 20 sites (a corridor deployment)**

| | Axles | Rate | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Band 1 | 500 | $600 | $300,000 |
| Band 2 | 1,500 | $500 | $750,000 |
| Band 3 | 3,000 | $375 | $1,125,000 |
| **Licence subtotal** | | | **$2,175,000** |
| Site fee (19 additional × $45,000) | | | $855,000 |
| **Annual total** | | | **$3,030,000** |

Example C is the number that must be shown to a customer considering a corridor deployment, and it is the number most vendors hide. At 40-mile detector spacing, a 2,200-mile corridor is roughly 34–55 sites. The site axis is not a rounding error on a corridor; at 55 sites it is $2,430,000 against a licence of $2,175,000. Roughly half the annual cost of a corridor deployment is geography, not assets. Stating that plainly is what makes the proposal credible.

### 3.4 Axle count changes during a term

**Increase.** The Railroad notifies us of the new count. The additional axles are priced at the applicable band rate, pro-rated from the first day of the following month to the end of the then-current term. No penalty, no renegotiation.

**Decrease.** Fees are not reduced retroactively. The new count applies from the next renewal anniversary.

**Reason:** the licence is a capacity commitment, not a usage meter. We provision and support for the committed count. A customer who wants true usage-based billing is asking for a different product, and it would price higher per axle because the volume risk moves to us.

---

## 4. Axis two — Per-site platform fee

| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| First site | **Included in the base licence** |
| Each additional site | **$45,000 per site per year** |

**What the site fee covers:** the edge server installation and configuration advisory, detector integration at that location, commissioning support, network path verification, per-site monitoring in the support queue, and the per-site quarterly performance report.

**Why it is separate from the axle fee.** Two deployments with identical axle counts are not the same job if one is a single classification yard and the other spans eleven subdivisions. Each location needs its own edge compute, its own integration, its own commissioning trip, and its own support coverage. Pricing geography as if it were a yard under-charges the work by an order of magnitude — and the shortfall only becomes visible after the deployment invoices arrive.

**What the site fee does not cover:** travel to the site (see §5.3), installation labour (the Railroad performs installation under D14), or on-site support beyond the included commissioning assistance.

---

## 4A. Axis three — the performance component (optional, offered only by election)

**This is not part of the base price and is not charged unless the Customer elects it in writing in the Order.**

D08 §4 describes a performance component: **3% of the cost of a prevented failure that the Customer's own root-cause analysis corroborates**, capped at **33% of the annual base licence**.

**Why it is an election and not a default:**

1. **It requires a corroboration process the Customer must operate.** Someone in the Customer's organisation has to attribute a prevented failure. That is real work, and it cannot be imposed.
2. **It is unenforceable without that process.** A performance fee on an uncorroboratable event is a disputed invoice waiting to happen.
3. **It is inappropriate during a pilot**, where the whole purpose is to discover whether the platform's assessments are worth acting on (D02 §8).

**If elected, the Order must state:** who corroborates, what evidence is required, the valuation method for a prevented failure, the reconciliation cadence, and the cap. Absent all five, the component is not operable and must not be included.

**Base pricing never depends on it.** A customer who declines the performance component pays the §3 and §4 rates and nothing more. A customer who elects it accepts additional upside **and** additional audit obligation. **Recommended default: do not offer it on a first pilot.** Offer it at first expansion, once the corroboration workflow has been proven on real events.

### 5.1 Pilot fees (D02)

| Component | Amount | Includes | Does not include |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **Pilot licence** (12 months, one site) | **$180,000** | Platform licence for one site, documentation, update packages during the term | Additional sites; production use |
| **Implementation support & commissioning assistance** | **$65,000** | Remote advisory support during the Railroad's installation; readiness review; commissioning checklist walkthrough | Installation labour; on-site attendance (see §5.3) |
| **Training materials & certification programme** | **$40,000** | Curriculum, assessment instruments, **manual certification register maintained per C02 §5**, up to 25 candidate assessments | Delivery of training itself; re-assessment of unsuccessful candidates (see §6); **software-side signed certification registry — not built (D09 §4.4, target Q2 2027)** |
| **Validation support** | **$35,000** | Historical data comparison, methodology review, written validation findings | Independent third-party validation |
| **Support during pilot** | **$50,000** | Defect correction, patches, licence and certification administration, per D06 §2 | Premium/out-of-hours support; custom development |
| **Total pilot fee** | **$370,000** | | |

**Payment schedule:** 40% ($148,000) on signature · 30% ($111,000) on Commissioning Date · 30% ($111,000) on completion of month six. Net thirty days. See Form F05 (Payment Terms Schedule).

**Conversion credit.** On conversion to a production licence under D05 within 90 days of pilot expiry, **50% of the pilot licence fee ($90,000)** is credited against the first production term. No other component is creditable. See §9 for the arithmetic.

### 5.2 Discovery and prototype fees (D04 SOW-3 and SOW-4)

| Service | Amount | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| **Feasibility & Physics Assessment** (discovery) | **$45,000 – $75,000** | Fixed fee, quoted per engagement based on asset class and data availability. 50% at Order signature, 50% on report delivery. |
| **Prototype development** | **$150,000 – $400,000** | Milestone-billed: 30% kickoff, 40% demonstration, 30% acceptance. Quoted per Order. |

Ranges are quoted rather than fixed because scope genuinely varies by failure mode and data quality. A fixed schedule with ranges is honest; a single number would be invented.

### 5.3 Travel and expenses

**On-site attendance is optional and is not included in any fixed fee.**

| Item | Basis |
|---|---|
| Airfare | Economy class, actual cost, no markup |
| Lodging | Standard business class hotel, actual cost, no markup |
| Meals and incidentals | Per diem at the applicable US GSA rate for the destination |
| Ground transport | Actual cost (rental, rideshare, parking) |
| **Pre-approval** | Required in writing before booking (Form F04) |
| **Cap per trip** | **$6,000** unless a higher cap is pre-approved in writing |
| **Receipts** | Required for all items; submitted within 14 days of return (Form F07) |

**Business development travel is never billable.** Flights to a corridor for a pre-contract conversation, a relationship meeting, or a capability briefing are our cost. Travel is billable only when it occurs because a customer asked us to attend their deployment under an executed Order.

**Book through the Railroad's travel system where required.** Many Class I carriers mandate this for vendor travel. Comply. It costs nothing and removes an audit objection.

### 5.4 Training and certification fees

| Item | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Curriculum and assessment package (one-time, per customer) | Included in pilot §5.1 |
| Additional candidate assessment beyond the 25 included | **$450 per candidate** |
| Re-assessment after a failed attempt | **$450 per candidate** |
| Recertification (on the three-year cycle, C02 §4.1) | **$200 per Reviewer** |
| On-site certification workshop (per day, plus travel under §5.3) | **$3,500 per day** |

### 5.5 Professional services (rate card)

| Role | Day rate |
|---|---:|
| Principal Systems Architect | **$2,400** |
| Senior Engineer | **$1,800** |
| Engineer | **$1,350** |
| Technical writer / training specialist | **$950** |
| Support engineer (extended or out-of-hours) | **$1,100** |

A day is eight hours. Travel days are billed at 50% of the applicable day rate where work is performed en route; travel days with no work are not billed.

**Professional services are always ordered by a written SOW (D04).** No professional services are performed on verbal instruction. This rule is not bureaucracy — it is what prevents the "small favour" from becoming an unbilled month.

---

## 6. What is included at no additional charge

Included in every active licence, pilot or production:

1. Software licence for the committed axle count and site count.
2. Documentation set (B01, B04, B05, C01, C02) in current version.
3. Defect correction and security patches, per D06 §3.
4. Support at the response times in D06 §2, during business hours.
5. Licence and certification registry administration.
6. Quarterly performance report (production licences only, D06 §5.1).
7. Data export in usable format at any time, and at termination (D07 §15.6).
8. Escrow deposit of the running version, per D13 §4.

**Nothing in this list is optional, and none of it is separately chargeable.** A customer who has to buy "support" as an add-on has been sold a licence they cannot operate.

---

## 7. What is not included

1. **Installation labour.** The Railroad installs. We advise (D14 §3). This is a liability boundary, not a cost saving.
2. **On-site attendance** beyond included commissioning assistance — priced per §5.3.
3. **Custom model development** or customer-specific physics models — priced per §5.5 under an Order.
4. **Major version upgrades** — priced per Order (D06 §3.5).
5. **Regulatory or audit support** — out of scope (D06 §1.2).
6. **Operating, dispatching, or inspection advice** — not merely out of scope; **prohibited** (D06 §1.4 as amended).
7. **Third-party software licences** required in the Railroad's environment.
8. **Taxes** — all fees are exclusive of sales, use, VAT, withholding, and similar (D02 §3.4).

---

## 8. Fee protection and increases

| Period | Protection |
|---|---|
| Pilot term | Fees fixed for the pilot term (D02 §3) |
| Production Years 1–3 | **0% increase** — locked at the converted rate (D05 §3.2) |
| Production Year 4 onward | Increase capped at **5% per year**, on 90 days' written notice |
| New sites added mid-term | Priced at the rate card in force at the date of the Order; locked for that site's initial term |
| Professional services day rates | Held for 12 months from the Effective Date; thereafter reviewed annually, cap 5% |

**Rates are held for the customer, not for us.** Once a customer has a signed Order, the rate in that Order does not move for its term regardless of what happens to this schedule. A rate card is a published offer, not a floating price.

---

## 9. Rollover arithmetic — worked example

A customer completes a 12-month pilot at one site, 500 axles, and converts within 90 days.

| Line | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Pilot fees already paid | $370,000 |
| — of which pilot licence | ($180,000) |
| **Year 1 production licence** (500 axles × $600) | **$300,000** |
| Site fee (first site) | $0 |
| **Gross Year 1 production fee** | **$300,000** |
| Less: pilot licence credit (50% × $180,000) | **–$90,000** |
| **Net Year 1 production fee** | **$210,000** |
| **Year 2** (locked, 0%) | $300,000 |
| **Year 3** (locked, 0%) | $300,000 |
| **Three-year net total after conversion** | **$810,000** |

**The number to show the CFO:** the customer's three-year net production cost is $810,000, against $370,000 already spent on the pilot — a total of $1,180,000 across four years for one site at 500 axles. If the modelled avoided-loss figure does not comfortably exceed that, the deal should not close, and saying so early is better than discovering it at the CFO's desk.

---

## 10. Invoicing and payment

1. **Currency:** USD.
2. **Terms:** net thirty days from invoice date.
3. **Method:** ACH or wire per the remittance details on the invoice. Never by card.
4. **Disputes:** a disputed line must be notified in writing within 15 days; undisputed lines remain payable.
5. **Late payment:** 1.0% per month on undisputed overdue amounts, or the maximum permitted by law if lower.
6. **Withholding:** the Railroad bears any required withholding and provides documentation sufficient for us to claim credit.
7. **Purchase orders:** where a PO number is required, it must be issued before the invoice, not after. An invoice without a valid PO is the most common cause of a 60-day payment delay.

---

## 11. Order of precedence

Where this schedule conflicts with any other document in the docket on a matter of **price**, this schedule governs. Where an executed Order states a price, the Order governs for that Order's scope and term. On every other matter, D07 governs generally and D02 governs during the pilot — see D00 Part IV.

---

## 12. Validity and change

This schedule takes effect on the Effective Date and remains in force until superseded. It may be revised on 90 days' written notice to customers with active Orders; **revisions never apply to an Order already in force.**

---

*This rate card is a commercial document, not legal advice. Executed Orders and counsel-reviewed contracts govern the relationship. All figures are in US dollars.*

Each location needs its own edge compute, its own integration, its own commissioning trip, and its own support coverage. Pricing geography as if it were a yard under-charges the work by an order of magnitude — and the shortfall only becomes visible after the deployment invoices arrive.
129	
130	**What the site fee does not cover:** travel to the site (see §5.3), installation labour (the Railroad performs installation under D14), or on-site support beyond the included commissioning assistance.
131	
132	---
133	
134	## 4A. Axis three — the performance component (optional, offered only by election)
135	
136	**This is not part of the base price and is not charged unless the Customer elects it in writing in the Order.**
137	
138	D08 §4 describes a performance component: **3% of the cost of a prevented failure that the Customer's own root-cause analysis corroborates**, capped at **33% of the annual base licence**.
139	
140	**Why it is an election and not a default:**
141	
142	1. **It requires a corroboration process the Customer must operate.** Someone in the Customer's organisation has to attribute a prevented failure. That is real work, and it cannot be imposed.
143	2. **It is unenforceable without that process.** A performance fee on an uncorroboratable event is a disputed invoice waiting to happen.
144	3. **It is inappropriate during a pilot**, where the whole purpose is to discover whether the platform's assessments are worth acting on (D02 §8).
145	
146	**If elected, the Order must state:** who corroborates, what evidence is required, the valuation method for a prevented failure, the reconciliation cadence, and the cap. Absent all five, the component is not operable and must not be included.
147	
148	**Base pricing never depends on it.** A customer who declines the performance component pays the §3 and §4 rates and nothing more. A customer who elects it accepts additional upside **and** additional audit obligation. **Recommended default: do not offer it on a first pilot.** Offer it at first expansion, once the corroboration workflow has been proven on real events.
149	
150	### 5.1 Pilot fees (D02)
151	
152	| Component | Amount | Includes | Does not include |
153	|---|---:|---|---|
154	| **Pilot licence** (12 months, one site) | **$180,000** | Platform licence for one site, documentation, update packages during the term | Additional sites; production use |
155	| **Implementation support & commissioning assistance** | **$65,000** | Remote advisory support during the Railroad's installation; readiness review; commissioning checklist walkthrough | Installation labour; on-site attendance (see §5.3) |
156	| **Training materials & certification programme** | **$40,000** | Curriculum, assessment instruments, **manual certification register maintained per C02 §5**, up to 25 candidate assessments | Delivery of training itself; re-assessment of unsuccessful candidates (see §6); **software-side signed certification registry — not built (D09 §4.4, target Q2 2027)** |
157	| **Validation support** | **$35,000** | Historical data comparison, methodology review, written validation findings | Independent third-party validation |
158	| **Support during pilot** | **$50,000** | Defect correction, patches, licence and certification administration, per D06 §2 | Premium/out-of-hours support; custom development |
159	| **Total pilot fee** | **$370,000** | | |
160	
161	**Payment schedule:** 40% ($148,000) on signature · 30% ($111,000) on Commissioning Date · 30% ($111,000) on completion of month six. Net thirty days. See Form F05 (Payment Terms Schedule).
162	
163	**Conversion credit.** On conversion to a production licence under D05 within 90 days of pilot expiry, **50% of the pilot licence fee ($90,000)** is credited against the first production term. No other component is creditable. See §9 for the arithmetic.
164	
165	### 5.2 Discovery and prototype fees (D04 SOW-3 and SOW-4)
166	
167	| Service | Amount | Notes |
168	|---|---:|---|
169	| **Feasibility & Physics Assessment** (discovery) | **$45,000 – $75,000** | Fixed fee, quoted per engagement based on asset class and data availability. 50% at Order signature, 50% on report delivery. |
170	| **Prototype development** | **$150,000 – $400,000** | Milestone-billed: 30% kickoff, 40% demonstration, 30% acceptance. Quoted per Order. |
171	
172	Ranges are quoted rather than fixed because scope genuinely varies by failure mode and data quality. A fixed schedule with ranges is honest; a single number would be invented.
173	
174	### 5.3 Travel and expenses
175	
176	**On-site attendance is optional and is not included in any fixed fee.**
177	
178	| Item | Basis |
179	|---|---|
180	| Airfare | Economy class, actual cost, no markup |
181	| Lodging | Standard business class hotel, actual cost, no markup |
182	| Meals and incidentals | Per diem at the applicable US GSA rate for the destination |
183	| Ground transport | Actual cost (rental, rideshare, parking) |
184	| **Pre-approval** | Required in writing before booking (Form F04) |
185	| **Cap per trip** | **$6,000** unless a higher cap is pre-approved in writing |
186	| **Receipts** | Required for all items; submitted within 14 days of return (Form F07) |
187	
188	**Business development travel is never billable.** Flights to a corridor for a pre-contract conversation, a relationship meeting, or a capability briefing are our cost. Travel is billable only when it occurs because a customer asked us to attend their deployment under an executed Order.
189	
190	**Book through the Railroad's travel system where required.** Many Class I carriers mandate this for vendor travel. Comply. It costs nothing and removes an audit objection.
191	
192	### 5.4 Training and certification fees
193	
194	| Item | Amount |
195	|---|---:|
196	| Curriculum and assessment package (one-time, per customer) | Included in pilot §5.1 |
197	| Additional candidate assessment beyond the 25 included | **$450 per candidate** |
198	| Re-assessment after a failed attempt | **$450 per candidate** |
199	| Recertification (on the three-year cycle, C02 §4.1) | **$200 per Reviewer** |
200	| On-site certification workshop (per day, plus travel under §5.3) | **$3,500 per day** |
201	
202	### 5.5 Professional services (rate card)
203	
204	| Role | Day rate |
205	|---|---:|
206	| Principal Systems Architect | **$2,400** |
207	| Senior Engineer | **$1,800** |
208	| Engineer | **$1,350** |
209	| Technical writer / training specialist | **$950** |
210	| Support engineer (extended or out-of-hours) | **$1,100** |
211	
212	A day is eight hours. Travel days are billed at 50% of the applicable day rate where work is performed en route; travel days with no work are not billed.
213	
214	**Professional services are always ordered by a written SOW (D04).** No professional services are performed on verbal instruction. This rule is not bureaucracy — it is what prevents the "small favour" from becoming an unbilled month.
215	
216	---
217	
218	## 6. What is included at no additional charge
219	
220	Included in every active licence, pilot or production:
221	
222	1. Software licence for the committed axle count and site count.
223	2. Documentation set (B01, B04, B05, C01, C02) in current version.
224	3. Defect correction and security patches, per D06 §3.
225	4. Support at the response times in D06 §2, during business hours.
226	5. Licence and certification registry administration.
227	6. Quarterly performance report (production licences only, D06 §5.1).
228	7. Data export in usable format at any time, and at termination (D07 §15.6).
229	8. Escrow deposit of the running version, per D13 §4.
230	
231	**Nothing in this list is optional, and none of it is separately chargeable.** A customer who has to buy "support" as an add-on has been sold a licence they cannot operate.
232	
233	---
234	
235	## 7. What is not included
236	
237	1. **Installation labour.** The Railroad installs. We advise (D14 §3). This is a liability boundary, not a cost saving.
238	2. **On-site attendance** beyond included commissioning assistance — priced per §5.3.
239	3. **Custom model development** or customer-specific physics models — priced per §5.5 under an Order.
240	4. **Major version upgrades** — priced per Order (D06 §3.5).
241	5. **Regulatory or audit support** — out of scope (D06 §1.2).
242	6. **Operating, dispatching, or inspection advice** — not merely out of scope; **prohibited** (D06 §1.4 as amended).
243	7. **Third-party software licences** required in the Railroad's environment.
244	8. **Taxes** — all fees are exclusive of sales, use, VAT, withholding, and similar (D02 §3.4).
245	
246	---
247	
248	## 8. Fee protection and increases
249	
250	| Period | Protection |
251	|---|---|
252	| Pilot term | Fees fixed for the pilot term (D02 §3) |
253	| Production Years 1–3 | **0% increase** — locked at the converted rate (D05 §3.2) |
254	| Production Year 4 onward | Increase capped at **5% per year**, on 90 days' written notice |
255	| New sites added mid-term | Priced at the rate card in force at the date of the Order; locked for that site's initial term |
256	| Professional services day rates | Held for 12 months from the Effective Date; thereafter reviewed annually, cap 5% |
257	
258	**Rates are held for the customer, not for us.** Once a customer has a signed Order, the rate in that Order does not move for its term regardless of what happens to this schedule. A rate card is a published offer, not a floating price.
259	
260	---
261	
262	## 9. Rollover arithmetic — worked example
263	
264	A customer completes a 12-month pilot at one site, 500 axles, and converts within 90 days.
265	
266	| Line | Amount |
267	|---|---:|
268	| Pilot fees already paid | $370,000 |
269	| — of which pilot licence | ($180,000) |
270	| **Year 1 production licence** (500 axles × $600) | **$300,000** |
271	| Site fee (first site) | $0 |
272	| **Gross Year 1 production fee** | **$300,000** |
273	| Less: pilot licence credit (50% × $180,000) | **–$90,000** |
274	| **Net Year 1 production fee** | **$210,000** |
275	| **Year 2** (locked, 0%) | $300,000 |
276	| **Year 3** (locked, 0%) | $300,000 |
277	| **Three-year net total after conversion** | **$810,000** |
278	
279	**The number to show the CFO:** the customer's three-year net production cost is $810,000, against $370,000 already spent on the pilot — a total of $1,180,000 across four years for one site at 500 axles. If the modelled avoided-loss figure does not comfortably exceed that, the deal should not close, and saying so early is better than discovering it at the CFO's desk.
280	
281	---
282	
283	## 10. Invoicing and payment
284	
285	1. **Currency:** USD.
286	2. **Terms:** net thirty days from invoice date.
287	3. **Method:** ACH or wire per the remittance details on the invoice. Never by card.
288	4. **Disputes:** a disputed line must be notified in writing within 15 days; undisputed lines remain payable.
289	5. **Late payment:** 1.0% per month on undisputed overdue amounts, or the maximum permitted by law if lower.
290	6. **Withholding:** the Railroad bears any required withholding and provides documentation sufficient for us to claim credit.
291	7. **Purchase orders:** where a PO number is required, it must be issued before the invoice, not after. An invoice without a valid PO is the most common cause of a 60-day payment delay.
292	
293	---
294	
295	## 11. Order of precedence
296	
297	Where this schedule conflicts with any other document in the docket on a matter of **price**, this schedule governs. Where an executed Order states a price, the Order governs for that Order's scope and term. On every other matter, D07 governs generally and D02 governs during the pilot — see D00 Part IV.
298	
299	---
300	
301	## 12. Validity and change
302	
303	This schedule takes effect on the Effective Date and remains in force until superseded. It may be revised on 90 days' written notice to customers with active Orders; **revisions never apply to an Order already in force.**
304	
305	---
306	
307	*This rate card is a commercial document, not legal advice. Executed Orders and counsel-reviewed contracts govern the relationship. All figures are in US dollars.*
308	
</system-reminder>

**AxiomDynamics** is a physics-first predictive maintenance product for freight rail. It uses six named physical models (thermodynamics with per-axle rolling z-score, peer median/MAD comparison, kinematics from E_k=½mv², acoustics via BPFO/BPFI/BSF/FTF, same-axle left/right differential, and an ROI panel) rather than black-box ML or fixed alarm thresholds.

**Repo:** `C:\Users\RGV\AxiomDynamics` · remote `github.com/kaanju19-lang/AxiomDynamics` (private).

**Structure:** `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/` holds 38 artifacts (36 Markdown plus the A1 `.xlsx` with its build script, plus B03 `.html`) covering 37 docket IDs — A (commercial A1–A2), B (technical B01–B05), C (deployment C01–C02), D (contractual D00–D14), F (forms F00–F13). `assets/` holds internal analysis. `project-logs/` holds the cross-session memory: `CURRENT-STATE.md`, `chat-1/`, `chat-2/`, `chat-3/`.

**Standing instructions from the user, still in force:**
- "We will keep this same concept throughout" — the physics-first framing and document structure do not vary between documents.
- "Strictly goes in our assets folder" — internal analysis in `assets/`, never `client-assets/`.

**Largest known gap:** there is no detector ingest path. No endpoint accepts a Railroad payload; all demonstration signals come from the physics equations on synthetic traces. Disclosed in B01 §7 gap #5, B02 §2, B03 status block.

**Working discipline:** verify against the file, then write. Every bad citation in this project came from writing a claim from memory and checking afterwards — and the worst defect, the ingest path drawn as built, came from the same habit applied to a diagram.

**Where it stood on 2026-11-09 (end of chat-2):** commits `f58b07c`, `c9b32bd`, `146b8e4` rebuilt the lost chat-1 work (F00 Rule 7, D07 §14.5 venue, Q6, project-logs) and were committed locally. **Push status unknown — verify before assuming GitHub has them.** Next task: the A2/D08 arithmetic pass, untouched since `cf2e6ba`.

**Where it stood at chat-3's close (2026-11-10).** **Chat-3 is closed.** Three builds landed: the append-only disposition ledger (AD-3 part one, `209efe6`), the signed ledger export (AD-3 part two, `d9c83d4`, HMAC-SHA256 with a standalone verifier in `tools/` that imports nothing from `backend/`), and the transcript machinery (`project-logs/extract_transcript.py`). Plus the A2/D08 decision paper (`b23d0c7`) which prices both open model findings. Suite is 80 tests: 21 physics, 17 ledger, 42 export. **Next session starts from `project-logs/chat-4/CARRY-FORWARD.md`** — read it first, then `CURRENT-STATE.md`, then confirm against git.

**The two findings are still open and still need the owner.** A1 governs the recommendation (0.05% escalation, $500,000 typical cost); options and the case against are in `assets/a2-d08-model-decision-2026-11-09.md` §6–§7. The decision paper refined Finding 1: the 2.0×/4.1× anchors **are** recoverable on an unstated cost basis (p between 0.04% and 0.07%), which makes it a disclosure defect rather than a fabrication — but it cannot ship until a frame is stated. A1's workbook is still deliberately not regenerated.

**Chat-4, phase one (2026-11-10) — ledger replication series, built and committed.** `backend/ledger_replication.py` produces the D09 §4.5.4 cadence itself: monthly full, weekly incremental chained by `previous_export_hash`, zero-record weeks kept, nothing overwritten. `inspect` opens every bundle, recomputes its digest, verifies it against the predecessor, and reports a missing period. Suite 80 → **112**. Commit `5ce18cd`, carry-forward `7116f64`.

**It deliberately transmits nothing.** D09 §3.2 promises the Platform has no outbound network, so off-box carriage stays the Railroad's physical step under §3.3. On 2026-11-10 the owner chose on-box scheduling + physical carriage over a network push. Both docket rows (B01 §7 item 12, D09 §4.4) now say carriage remains open instead of implying replication is finished.

**Two audits found nine material defects before it was called built — carry this shape forward.** The standalone release verifier rejected every legitimate chained full export while the in-repo one passed; `inspect` originally never opened a bundle, so tampering read as "continuous"; the period walker **hung forever** on a 53-week ISO year (2026 is one); `due_exports` read state outside the lock so concurrent runs duplicated bundles; and one test passed only because the check it guarded had been deleted. A green suite of 108 preceded all of it. Full record: `assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**Nearest build if the decision stays deferred:** off-box replication of the ledger (B01 §7 item 12, D09 §4.4–4.5). **Not** signer attribution — that is a genuine AD-2 dependency (real local accounts, a key per reviewer), much larger than it looks.

**Repo quirk that wastes time if forgotten:** `git status` in this repo lists nearly every tracked file as modified on a fresh Windows checkout — CRLF working tree vs LF blobs, not content. No `.gitattributes`, `core.autocrlf` unset. Always check with `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol`. An editor round-trip rewrote a builder to CRLF during chat-3 and turned a 2-line fix into 1,248 changed lines; that had to be reset and recommitted.

See [[axiomdynamics-work-in-repo-only]] for the write-location rule, [[axiomdynamics-build-history-doc]] for the build history the owner commissioned (now 32 pages, carrying Stages 0–7), and [[axiomdynamics-preserve-transcripts]] for the transcript rule.

# Chat-4 — Carry-Forward

Handoff from chat-3, closed 2026-11-10. Read this first, then confirm every
claim below against the repository. **Nothing in this document is authority.**
The repository is. Every written push list in this project has gone stale at
least once, including three in chat-3's own record.

---

## Read in this order

1. `project-logs/CURRENT-STATE.md` — what is built, what is pushed, what is open.
2. This file — where chat-3 stopped and what it left waiting.
3. `project-logs/chat-3/SUMMARY.md` — the reasoning behind each phase.
4. `project-logs/AxiomDynamics-Build-History-and-Working-Summary.docx` — 32
   pages, the whole build, readable cold. Regenerate it with
   `node project-logs/build-history-summary.js` after any material change; do
   not hand-edit the .docx.
5. `client-assets/MASTER-BRIEF-DOCKET/D00-DOCKET-INDEX.md`, Part IV and Part VI —
   the authority on docket status and the gap register.

## Confirm state, do not assume it

```bash
git log --oneline -8                            # where chat-3 stopped
git status --short --branch                     # how far ahead of the remote ref
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD             # what is actually unpushed
git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat              # real changes only
python3 -I tests/run_tests.py                   # 80 passed, 0 failed at close
```

**The line-ending trap.** `git status` lists nearly every tracked file as
modified on this checkout. It is CRLF working-tree content against LF blobs, not
content: `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` returns empty for those. There is no
`.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf` is unset. Always check with
`--ignore-cr-at-eol`, stage named files only, and **never `git add -A`**.

## Push required before anything else

The command environment cannot reach GitHub — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail
with HTTP 403 from the proxy. The owner pushes with `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the
repo root, and then confirms on the commits page. Until that happens, none of it
is durable anywhere but this disk.

**Check the queue with `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`; do not trust a
number written here.** At chat-4's close of this phase the local branch stood two
commits ahead of its own `origin/main` ref (`548ab32`, `5ce18cd`), and the ref
itself is not evidence of what the remote holds, because the sandbox cannot
fetch.

## Chat-4 phase one — the replication series (built, audited, committed)

`5ce18cd`. `backend/ledger_replication.py` produces the D09 §4.5.4 cadence and
verifies it; it deliberately transmits nothing, because D09 §3.2 promises no
outbound network, so carriage is the Railroad's physical step. Full record,
including all nine defects two audits found, in
`assets/ledger-replication-build-2026-11-10.md`.

**The version of this file below was written at chat-3's close and its push
section is stale — the rest of it still stands.** Everything from "What chat-3
built" down remains an accurate account of the preceding session.

## Chat-3's close, as written then

The command environment cannot reach GitHub — `git push` and `git fetch` both fail
with HTTP 403 from the proxy. Chat-3 ended with commits local and unpushed on top
of a remote ref of `bb99cdd`. The owner pushes with `PUSH-TO-GITHUB.bat` in the
repo root, and then confirms on the commits page. Until that happens, none of it
is durable anywhere but this disk.

## What chat-3 built

Four substantive phases and a transcript phase. Full reasoning in

- Facts you can re-derive from the filesystem (file locations, project structure you could just re-read) or re-fetch from a connected tool.
- Anything already documented in CLAUDE.md files.
- Ephemeral task details: analysis results, in-progress work, temporary state, current conversation context.

These exclusions apply even when the user explicitly asks you to save. If they ask you to save a meeting recap or an inbox summary, ask what was *surprising* or *non-obvious* about it — that is the part worth keeping.

## How to save memories

**Write early, write often.** Memory writes are cheap; rediscovery is expensive. Don't wait for a clean stopping point — there isn't one. Good moments to write include:
- figuring out why something was broken or behaving unexpectedly
- learning a fact, constraint, or config detail that wasn't obvious from the code/docs
- making a non-trivial decision (record the *why*, not just the what)
- discovering that an approach *doesn't* work — negative results save future time too
- finishing a sub-task or switching context
- noticing you've been working >15-20 min without saving anything
- finishing research (even partially)

**Err toward writing.** If you're unsure whether something is worth saving, save it — a slightly noisy memory is far better than an empty one.

Saving a memory is a two-step process:

**Step 1** — write the memory to its own file (e.g., `user_role.md`, `feedback_testing.md`) using this frontmatter format:

```markdown
---
name: {{memory name — other memories can reference this one inline as [[name]]}}
description: {{one-line description — used to decide relevance in future conversations, so be specific}}
type: {{user, feedback, project, reference}}
---

{{memory content — for feedback/project types, structure as: rule/fact, then **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Use [[name]] to reference other memories by their name field. [[name]] should match filename.}}
```

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is the index and, when there is one, is loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise. If no index is loaded, `MEMORY.md` was missing or empty when this conversation started.
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- **Maintain it.** If something in memory turns out to be wrong or outdated, correct it immediately — stale memory is worse than no memory.

## Before applying/recommending a memory

Check if the memory applies - some guidance is only specific to a particular type of workflow/deliverable, DO NOT extrapolate. When in doubt, ask the user.

Memory records what was true at write time. Docs get edited, tickets get reassigned, threads get new replies. When a memory points at something you can refetch, verify it before the user acts on it.

- **Doc or page** → open it. Content may have changed.
- **Ticket, task, or link** → re-read from the source when you can.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

## Sensitive personal information

Do not save the following to memory unless the user explicitly asks you to remember it:

- Protected attributes: race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration status, disability, serious illness, union membership
- Government identifiers: Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport numbers, government ID numbers
- Financial account details: credit card numbers, bank account numbers
- Health information: medical conditions, diagnoses, lab results, mental health details, therapy or counseling
- Home or personal mailing addresses (work addresses are fine)

If any of the above appears in conversation context, complete the task but do not persist it to a memory file. If the user explicitly says "remember my address is X", saving it is acceptable — they've given consent.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here. Every Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** The tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. You get a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching, you know nothing about what the fork found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>
Agent({
  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
</example>

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Agent tool instead (if available)

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool (if available) for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskCreate
tools.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

description.description: What needs to be done

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

tools.name: TaskGet
tools.description:
Use this tool to retrieve a task by its ID from the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- When you need the full description and context before starting work on a task
- To understand task dependencies (what it blocks, what blocks it)
- After being assigned a task, to get complete requirements

## Output

Returns full task details:
- **subject**: Task title
- **description**: Detailed requirements and context
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **blocks**: Tasks waiting on this one to complete
- **blockedBy**: Tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Tips

- After fetching a task, verify its blockedBy list is empty before beginning work.
- Use TaskList to see all tasks in summary form.

taskId.description: The ID of the task to retrieve

tools.name: TaskList
tools.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: TaskUpdate
tools.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
- Allows Claude to search the web and use the results to inform responses
- Provides up-to-date information for current events and recent data
- Returns search result information formatted as search result blocks, including links as markdown hyperlinks
- Use this tool for accessing information beyond Claude's knowledge cutoff
- Searches are performed automatically within a single API call

CRITICAL REQUIREMENT - You MUST follow this:
  - After answering the user's question, you MUST include a "Sources:" section at the end of your response
  - In the Sources section, list all relevant URLs from the search results as markdown hyperlinks: [Title](URL)
  - This is MANDATORY - never skip including sources in your response
  - Example format:

    [Your answer here]

    Sources:
    - [Source Title 1](https://example.com/1)
    - [Source Title 2](https://example.com/2)

Usage notes:
  - Domain filtering is supported to include or block specific websites
  - Web search is only available in the US

IMPORTANT - Use the correct year in search queries:
  - The current month is (provided in the conversation below). You MUST use this year when searching for recent information, documentation, or current events.
  - Example: If the user asks for "latest React docs", search for "React documentation" with the current year, NOT last year

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__cowork__allow_cowork_file_delete
